genericRisk: Three giveaways. First, the colour system: a neutral warm paper plus exactly one "trust blue" (`--c-corporate: #1f4f73`, §6.1) is the default move of every tool-shaped webapp of the last five years. In an app whose subject is colour it is worse than generic, it is interference — §6.1 puts that blue and its soft tint on the selected plan row, the active segment and the active tab, i.e. directly around the swatches I am trying to match. Selection and focus in this app should be achromatic (graphite field, heavier rule, bolder number); the only hue on screen should be paint. Second, the uniform hint line: §8.8 makes `control__hint` part of the anatomy of every row, and §9.5 duly fills fourteen of them. Read as a page, Setup becomes generated documentation — a painter reads each of those sentences once and then has to scroll past them forever. Make the hint available per group or on first run and let the control rows be short after that. Third, `AI help` as one of five top-level Setup groups (§8.8, §9.5) is 2025 webapp furniture in a studio tool; it belongs next to Account at the bottom, not level with `Plan` and `Photo`. Smaller tells: `plan__count` reading `5 layers, 2 accents, 11 steps · match: good` (§9.3) is a software status line, and the readout state `tap the picture again to clear` (§8.3) is the app talking about itself. Credit where due: the document avoids the usual traps honestly — no emoji, no shadows except dialogs (§6.3), no uppercase, no icon soup, and copy written in sentences rather than labels.
keep: §2.2, one plan model. Making a mix and a layer the same kind of row — number, swatch, paint line, meta line, bar — is the best idea in the document and the one I would defend hardest. It matches how I actually work: a plan is a list of things to paint in order, and the method only changes what is in the bucket. Deleting LayerStrip.vue (§11) because the structure removes its reason to exist is the right kind of deletion.

§5, the gesture table. Every hover, double-click and precise drag in the current build is named with its replacement, and the replacement is a labelled button, not a cleverer gesture. The tap-to-place close-up frame with four 48 px corner handles and a `Use this detail` / `Cancel` bar is exactly how a framing tool should work with a damp glove on.

§8.3, the readout line with reserved height and a never-empty rule. Replacing the pointer tooltip with one fixed line under the picture is correct, and reserving the 2.75rem so nothing jumps when it fills is the kind of detail that only shows up when someone has actually watched a page move under their hand.

§8.8, the control row: label, right-aligned tabular value, minus, slider, plus, hint. A 30 px thumb with a 48 px band and a stepper at each end means I can set Colours to exactly 14 without a dragging contest. This is the single biggest practical improvement over the current build.

§8.7, the detail card in page flow with floating.js deleted. A panel that covers the picture while I am looking at the picture is indefensible, and the spec kills it outright rather than making the drag better.

§9 as a whole: every string written out, in sentences, no symbols standing in for words. §9.3's layer meta `1:4 with water, like tea · 3 coats · 23% · for the darks` is the only line in the whole document that sounds like it was written by someone who has loaded a brush, and the wash key `W very watery · L light · M medium · R rich · C concentrated` (§8.6, §9.3) means the letters on the wash bar are not a private code.

§7, the typeface argument. Choosing on `1 / l / I` and `0 / O` because the screen is full of three-digit paint numbers read at an angle, and rejecting Inter on its bare capital I rather than on taste, is the right way to make that decision. `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` on values and not on running text is correct.
§11 and §13. A per-file migration table and ten checkable acceptance criteria make this a document someone can build from and be held to. Most design specs stop before this part.
mustFix: §4.1 and §14.2 — the phone layout does not fit on a phone, by its own numbers. Add up what §4.1 pins into the sticky region: app bar 3.25rem (52), stage tools 3rem (48), canvas 42dvh, viewbar 3rem (48), toggles row 3rem (48), readout 2.75rem (44), plus the 8 px gaps between them, and then the fixed tab bar 3.5rem (56) plus the home indicator. On a 390x844 iPhone that leaves 142 px for the panel region — two and a half plan rows of 3.5rem. On a 375x667 iPhone SE it leaves 39 px, which is nothing at all. §14.2 states "42 dvh leaves roughly 300 px of panel": that is wrong by a factor of two because it counted the picture and forgot the six bars the same section stacks around it. So §3.3, the loop the brief says the current build fails — tap area 12, read the recipe, picture and recipe both on screen — cannot happen: the detail card alone (two 3.5rem compare fields with captions, an actions row, a recipe list) is taller than the space left. Fix the structure, not the number: on phone collapse `stage__tools`, the viewbar and the toggles into ONE 48 px row inside the stage (the view switch as the segmented control, `Fit`, `Outlines`, `Numbers` behind a single `Show` button that opens a small sheet), cap the canvas at about 30dvh with the readout directly beneath it, and state the resulting budget in px for 667, 844 and 932 tall screens. Then re-check criterion 1 in §13 against those numbers.

§4.1, phone landscape, is specified to overflow. The rule gives the canvas `max-height: calc(100dvh - 3.25rem - 3.5rem - 2rem)` = 250 px on an 844x390 screen, but the stage column also carries the tools row, the viewbar, the toggles row and the readout: 52 + 48 + 250 + 48 + 48 + 44 = 490 px inside a 390 px viewport. The picture scrolls away again, which is the exact failure the section claims to beat. In landscape the canvas must be sized from what is left after the stage's own chrome, not from the viewport, and the toggles belong in the right-hand column with the panel.

§8.9 and §6.1 — the primary button is unreadable in dark mode, which is the evening-in-the-studio case the brief declares required. §8.9 defines `button` (primary) as `--c-corporate` on `--c-white`; in dark mode `--c-corporate` is `#8fbfe3`, so that is white text on pale blue: 1.96:1. The contrast paragraph in §6.1 measures text against surfaces and never checks ink on `--c-corporate`, so the error survived. Add a token (`--c-corporate-ink`: `#ffffff` light, `#141210` dark) and apply it to the primary button, and state the measured ratio for every ink-on-fill pair, not only text-on-surface. `New photo`, `Update mixes` and `Next` in the step walk are all this button.

§8.6 — the swatch, the one object on the screen I actually hold a wet brush next to, has no size anywhere in the document. `plan__swatch` is listed as an element, but the row geometry declares only three columns, `[tick] 3rem [number] 2.5rem [body] minmax(0, 1fr)`, with no column for it; §8.7 lists `detail__swatch` and never sizes it either; the only measurement given is that the `detail__compare` cells are 3.5rem tall. A 56 px high patch is too small to judge a mix against, and "it is somewhere in the body column" is not buildable. Specify it: a 3rem square minimum in the plan row (same height as the row's touch target), and in the detail card two fields of at least 5rem height each, sitting on white with a 1 px neutral rule between them and nothing coloured within a finger's width. Say explicitly that the mix field is drawn at the wash strength on white paper, not at masstone, because that is what I compare against.

§8.3, the readout precedence table, gives the recipe to the mouse and withholds it from the finger. Hovering with a fine pointer produces `12 · 23% of image · 1 x 663 Sepia brown + 2 x 485 Indigo`. Selecting by tap — the primary device, per the brief — produces `Colour 12 selected · 23% of image · tap the picture again to clear`. So on the iPad the readout replaces the paint names with a sentence about how to undo a tap. Invert it: a selection must render the same recipe string as hover, and the clear instruction belongs in the detail card's close affordance, not in the one line I read from across the table.

§8.5 and §4.1 — the step walk, the only part of the app that answers "what do I do while this wash dries", has no phone layout. §3.4 specifies it for iPad landscape, §8.5 defines the block, and the phone diagram in §4.1 shows a viewbar and no steps at all; §8.5 says the open state "replaces the viewbar inside the stage", which on a phone means a title, a three-option segmented control, a hint line, three labelled lines and two 56 px buttons — about 300 px — dropped into a sticky region that has 142 px to spare. State the phone step layout explicitly: picture capped at about 26dvh, `Step 3 of 11` with the `Mix` / `Paint` / `Then` lines in the panel region, and `Previous` / `Next` as 56 px buttons pinned above the tab bar where a thumb reaches them. Note that today's `Then` line already says `let it dry completely` (LayerSteps.vue:37) and keep that sentence visible without scrolling, because it is the instruction I obey most often.

No confirmation is specified for anything destructive, while §4.2 puts the destructive buttons 8 px from the ones I touch constantly. On iPad portrait the photo actions become "a right-aligned wrap row of six 48 px buttons" in the stage head — `New photo` and `Sample`, both of which throw away a plan I may have spent twenty minutes tuning, sit in the same row as `Save` and `Print / PDF`, directly above the picture I tap all day, with gloves on. §8.11 puts `Delete box` next to `New box` and `Rename` in the paint box's first body row; §8.14 puts 48 px `Delete` buttons on every collection thumbnail. §6.1 reserves `--c-danger` for "errors, destructive confirmations" and §8.9 defines `button--danger`, but no confirmation dialog is defined anywhere, so a builder will ship none. Specify one confirm pattern (title, what is lost in plain words, `button--danger` primary, `Cancel` as the safe default), say which actions raise it (`New photo` and `Sample` when the current plan is unsaved, `Delete box`, `Delete` in the collection, `Clear` in the paint box), and separate the destructive photo actions from `Save` / `Print` into their own group with more than 8 px between the groups.
shouldFix: §8.8 specifies a performance trap in writing: "Steppers apply exactly one `step` per tap" and "fire the same `change` handler as the slider, so the analysis re-runs once per tap". Taking Colours from 2 to 20 is eighteen full re-analyses queued on an iPad. Either the stepper must commit on a short idle (say 400 ms after the last tap) or the slider must commit on release only; say which, because §5 also promises immediate tap feedback and those two rules fight.

§9.3 puts the actual painting instruction in the faintest type on the screen. `1:4 with water, like tea` is what I need while mixing, and it lives in `plan__meta`: `--fs-small` (14 px on a phone) in `--c-copy-light`, which measures 5.94:1 on `--c-surface-sunken` and 5.63:1 on its dark equivalent — below the 6.4:1 §6.1 claims, because §6.1 measured it on plain surfaces and not on the sunken rows where the hovered and inset rows actually sit. Promote the water ratio and the consistency word into the row's primary line at `--fs-copy` in `--c-copy`, and leave the percentage and the coat count in the meta.

§8.6 sets `plan__number` at `--fs-medium` (18 px on a phone, 20 px on desktop) at weight 600, which is smaller than a card title (`--fs-large`) and far smaller than a dialog title. The number is the single thing I look up most, usually from a metre away with the iPad flat on the table. Give it `--fs-hl-small` with the swatch beside it; nothing else in the row needs to grow.

§2.3 and §4.1 contradict each other. §2.3 promises that Areas, Saturation, Contrast and the reset are first level, "on screen or one tap away, on every device, without scrolling past anything". §4.1 puts all of Setup in one tab as five stacked groups, so on a phone Saturation sits in group four, below Method, Plan and Shapes. Either state honestly that Setup is a scroll on the phone, or give the Settings tab a sticky group bar so the five group names are one tap each.

§8.11, the paint box, ignores how many paints there are. 54 chips in `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(9rem, 1fr))` is two columns at 375 px, so 27 rows of 3.5rem — roughly 1500 px of scrolling inside a full-screen dialog — and there is no way to find `663 Sepia brown` except by eye. Add a filter field at the top of `dialog__body` (48 px, matches on number, English name and `nameDe`) and keep `Selected paints` pinned above it. Second problem: at `min(60rem, …)` the dialog covers the picture and the plan, and `Update mixes` is in `dialog__foot`, so the loop "tick this paint, see what it does to the plan" needs a close and a reopen each time. Say whether the plan updates live behind the dialog or state that the painter must close it.

Nothing in §8.8 or §9.5 says what happens to my hand-changed colours when I move a slider. The plan rows are allowed to read `changed` (§9.3) and the detail card offers `Change colour` and `Back to photo colour` (§9.4), but a re-analysis re-derives the entries; the store tries to re-attach overrides by matching (`src/stores/analysis.js:807-811`) and silently drops the ones it cannot match. Overruling the maths is the whole reason I am here, and I will not touch Simplify again if it quietly eats my edits. Specify the behaviour and the warning: a hint on the Plan group, and a line in the plan card after a recompute naming how many hand-changed colours were kept.

§8.12 adds 5.5rem of close-up strip under the readout and §4.1 never accounts for it. The moment I pick one detail, the phone's sticky region grows by 88 px and the panel region drops to about 54 px on a 390x844 screen. Either the strip is horizontal and 3rem tall on the phone, or it lives in the `Photo` tab; decide in §4.1, not in §8.12.

§9.1 and §9.2 use the word `Photo` for three different things on one screen: the fourth tab (six file actions), a view option (`Photo`), and a second view option (`Photo colour`). §14.3 catches the `Details` collision and misses this one, which is worse because the tab and the view sit 100 px apart. Rename the tab to `Picture` or `Source`; the view options are the painter's language and should keep their names.

The printed sheet is the only artefact that survives a wet studio, and §10 and §11 leave `PrintLegend.vue`, `legend.css` and `layersheet.css` as they are apart from token renames. The whole document redesigns the screen I will be looking at through a smear and does not spend one paragraph on the page I will clip to the board. At minimum: state that the legend carries the wash key from §8.6, the water ratios from §9.3, and a blank box beside each number so I can tick off what is painted.

Nothing anywhere records what I have already painted. Eleven steps take an afternoon with drying between them; I put the phone down, come back, and the app has no idea where I was. §8.5 gives `Previous` / `Next` and no persisted position, and the plan rows have no painted state (`plan__item--current` marks only the open step). Add a `Painted` tick on the plan row and persist the step index — and say in §11 which existing store key holds it, since store APIs may not change.

§14.3 is right and should simply be decided: `Details` for the variety slider, `Detail 2` for a close-up and the AI's "details" cannot all stay. Rename the slider `Variety` in round 2 rather than carrying the question forward.
verdict: This is a serious document — the most buildable design spec I have been handed for this app, with real ideas in it — and the screen the owner complained about is still broken, by the specification's own arithmetic. Section 2.2 is genuinely good: one plan, two kinds of row, so switching method does not switch the interface. Section 5 kills every hover, double-click and precise drag by name and replaces each with a labelled button. Section 8.8 finally makes the sliders usable with gloves. Section 9 writes out every string, and one of them, "1:4 with water, like tea", reads like it came from someone who has loaded a brush. I would defend all of that in an argument. But §4.1 stacks six fixed bars around a 42dvh picture and then claims in §14.2 that 300 px of panel is left; the real figure is 142 px on an iPhone 14 and 39 px on an SE. So the one loop the brief says must work — tap area 12, read its recipe, picture and recipe both on screen — cannot fit, and §13's first acceptance criterion contradicts §4.1's own numbers. Phone landscape is specified to overflow its viewport by 100 px. The step walk, the part that answers "what do I do while this wash dries", has no phone layout at all. In dark mode the primary button is white text on pale blue at 1.96:1, because §6.1 checked text on surfaces and never checked ink on a fill. And the swatch — the thing I hold a wet brush beside, the reason this app exists — has no size anywhere in the document, no column in the plan row's grid, and no statement that the mix is drawn at wash strength on white; meanwhile §6.1 puts a blue tint behind the selected row, right next to the colour I am trying to judge. The desktop and iPad-landscape halves of this are close to ready. The phone is a sketch with wrong sums under it, which is exactly the complaint. Fix the arithmetic first, in px, for 667, 844 and 932 tall screens, and let the structure follow from the budget instead of the other way round. As it stands I would plan on this at the table and I would not trust it on the easel, so no, not yet on a good sheet of paper.

genericRisk: Not generic in intent — the warm paper/slate-blue palette, no gradients, no pills, no icon soup, drawn SVG favicon and the "only the photo and the paint are saturated" rule are real decisions, and §7's font argument is made on letterform grounds rather than taste. Three things still give it away. (1) The silhouette — a fixed top bar, rounded 12px white cards on a tinted page, segmented controls, a four-label bottom tab bar — is the current default shape of a considered-looking webapp; nothing in the layout, the type or the card structure says "watercolour workbench" except the background hex. The stage card in particular has no structure of its own: it is a white rectangle with a toolbar. (2) The design states "--c-corporate appears on at most the selected plan row, the active segment, the focus ring, and one primary button" (§6.1), then spends --c-corporate-soft on active tabs (§4.1), selected rows (§8.6), active segments (§8.9) and chosen recipes (§8.7) — a pale blue wash across four surface types at once, which is exactly the accent-everywhere habit the brief bans, just in one hue instead of eight. (3) The strongest tell is in the writing, not the pixels: the ASCII diagrams in §4.1 contradict the prose they illustrate (a "Detail" button that §9.2 calls "Pick a detail", no close-up strip, no step bar), §14.2 states a 300 px figure that was never computed, and §6.1 publishes four verified contrast ratios while quietly excluding the text that actually sits on paint colours. Numbers that look checked but are not is the AI-built signature here, more than any colour choice.
keep: §2.2 'One plan model' is the best thing in the document and the one part I would defend in an argument. Declaring the mix/layer difference once as a slot table — title, count line, leading control, number, swatch, name, meta, bar 1, bar 2, row tap, bar tap, detail card, header action — and rendering both from one `plan` block genuinely collapses the two universes instead of restyling them. It is also honest about the consequence: `LayerStrip.vue` is deleted because its reason to exist is gone, not because it was ugly.

§9 'Copy' as a complete string inventory, written in the product's own voice. 'Higher gives fewer and bigger shapes to paint', '1:4 with water, like tea', 'Leave the paper white.' An implementer does not have to invent a single label, and the hints replace the tooltips with text a painter can actually use rather than with an info icon.

§5's gesture table pairs every removed gesture with a named fallback (double-click reset becomes a labelled button, the pointer tip becomes the readout line, arrow-key stepping becomes 56 px Previous/Next with the key handler kept as an extra). That is the right discipline, and deleting `floating.js` outright rather than making the floating panel touch-friendly is the correct, unsentimental call.

§11's per-file migration table. It names real files, says what moves where, and states what must not change (`SCALE`, `regionAtCanvasPixel`, `drawMixes`, `drawLayers`, `drawSketch`, the stores, `src/lib/`). The build order is derivable from it.

§8.3's `picture__readout` as a fixed-height line that is never empty, with a precedence table for its content. It replaces a hover-only tooltip with something a gloved user can read, and reserving the space so nothing jumps is the kind of detail that only shows up when someone has actually watched a layout reflow.

§10's print claim is true and I checked it: `_legend.css` and `_layersheet.css` contain zero `rem` values, so dropping the `html { font-size: 10px }` hack does not break them. The spec asserted something verifiable and it verified.
mustFix: §4.1 and §14.2 — the phone vertical budget is wrong by two to three times, and it is the number the whole phone design rests on. Add the sticky region as specified: app bar 3.25rem (52) + stage padding 8 + `stage__tools` 3rem (48) + canvas 42dvh + viewbar row 1 3rem (48) + viewbar row 2 3rem (48) + `picture__readout` 2.75rem (44) + stage padding 8, with the fixed tab bar 3.5rem (56) + safe-area inset below. On a 390x844 iPhone in Safari, where the live viewport is about 734 px, 42dvh is 308 px and the chrome is 332 px, leaving roughly 95 px of panel region — not the 'roughly 300 px' §14.2 claims. §3.3 therefore fails its own acceptance test: tapping Recipe cannot put 'both on screen at once' when `detail__compare` alone is two 3.5rem fields plus captions plus a hex line plus three 48 px action buttons plus up to five 3.5rem recipe cards. Fix inside this design: only the app bar, the canvas and a one-line readout stay sticky. Move `viewbar` (both rows, 96 px) out of the sticky region into the top of the panel region, cap the whole sticky block at 46 % of the viewport, and set the canvas to about 32dvh on phone. Then recompute the number in §14.2 instead of calling it 'worth testing'.

§4.2 and §4.3 — the same arithmetic breaks the primary device. iPad portrait makes the stage sticky at `top: 3.5rem` with a 48dvh canvas and now also carries the photo actions in `stage__head`: on an 820x1180 iPad that is 56 + ~112 (name plus a wrap row of six 48 px buttons) + 48 + 96 + 44 + 88 (close-up strip) + 566 canvas, about 1010 px of a 1180 px screen, leaving roughly 170 px for a two-column region holding the detail card, the plan list and five settings groups. At §4.3 the reserved chrome is `calc(100dvh - 16rem)` = 256 px, but `stage__tools` + viewbar + readout + close-up strip is already about 324 px, so on a 1024x768 iPad landscape the sticky stage is taller than the viewport and stops being sticky at all. Either make `stage__head`, the close-up strip and the second viewbar row non-sticky, or state a single `--stage-chrome` token per breakpoint, compute the canvas from it, and give the stage a `max-height` that cannot exceed 60 % of the viewport. Phone landscape (§4.1, last bullet) fails the same way: a canvas of `calc(100dvh - 3.25rem - 3.5rem - 2rem)` plus 188 px of chrome needs 444 px in a column that has 282 px.

§8.9 and §6.1 — the primary button is illegible in dark mode. '`button` (primary) = `--c-corporate` on `--c-white`' with the dark values `--c-corporate: #8fbfe3` and `--c-white: #ffffff` gives about 2.0:1; `button--danger` = `--c-danger` #e4867a with `--c-white` gives 2.6:1. The other reading of 'A on B' is worse, because §6.1 says `--c-white` is 'never a surface'. §6.1's sentence 'Everything clears 4.5:1' is false for the two most important controls in the app. Add `--c-on-corporate` (light `#ffffff`, dark `#10212c`) and `--c-on-danger` (light `#ffffff`, dark `#2a0f0b`), state them in the §6.1 table, and use them in §8.9. While in there: §5 says the active state is 'one step darker (`--c-corporate-hover` for primary)', but in dark mode `--c-corporate-hover` #b3d6f0 is lighter than `--c-corporate` — say 'one step toward the surface' and keep the token.

§5 touch table versus §13.3 — 'Wash / coat segment | height: 2.5rem' is 40 px, below the brief's 48 px floor and below this document's own acceptance criterion 3. These are not decorative: §2.2 makes them the control that selects a wash and jumps to a step, and they sit in a row with other targets. Either give the segment a 3rem hit area with a 2.5rem painted band (padding on the button, not on the bar), or move wash selection into the detail card and make the bar a non-interactive `role="img"` as `palette__bar` already is in `PaletteList.vue`. Do not leave a table in §5 that the acceptance criteria in §13 contradict.

§8.6, §8.7 and the whole document — accessibility stops at the focus ring, and the brief asked specifically how a numbered colour list reads to a screen reader. The spec never says what element a `plan__item` is. §5 says 'whole row tappable', §2.2 adds a `Show` checkbox in layer mode and tappable bar segments inside the same row: that is three interactive controls in one 'tappable row', which cannot be a button containing buttons. Today `LayerList.vue` solves it (checkbox outside, `button.layers__row` inside, `aria-pressed`, `role="img"` on the bar) and that solution is thrown away unnamed. Specify per row: the tag, the accessible name pattern ('Colour 7, 1 part 663 Sepia brown plus 2 parts 485 Indigo, 23 percent of the image, 4 washes'), `aria-pressed` or `aria-current` for selected and for `--current`, and `role="img"` plus `aria-label` on both bars. Add the two live regions the design has no substitute for: the stage status slot ('Analysing…', §5) and `picture__readout` (§8.3) must be `aria-live="polite"`, or a blind or low-vision user gets no signal that anything happened. State focus order per breakpoint and focus return on dialog close.

§4.1, §8.6 and §8.7 — state is carried in colour alone in the three places it matters. The selected plan row is `background: var(--c-corporate-soft)` with a `--c-corporate` number and the spec explicitly forbids the alternative: 'no left border, no outline on the row itself'. The `Recipe` tab's pending selection is 'a dot (6px, --c-corporate) after the label', 6 px of colour with no text. `plan__item--current` and `plan__item--muted` are likewise background-only. The left-border ban is about decorative accent rules, not about every border: give the selected row a 1 px `--c-corporate` outline (as §8.7 already allows for `detail__recipe--chosen`) plus the word `selected` appended to `plan__meta`, mark `--muted` with the existing copy 'Not needed for this picture', and replace the tab dot with the word the tab is about to show, e.g. `Recipe 12`.

§9.6 and §11 — on the phone, every error and every busy signal lands in a tab the user is not looking at. `analysis.error` ('Could not load image: …', `analysis.js:297`) is specified to appear 'in a `--c-danger` line at the top of the plan card', but the user who tapped `New photo` is in the `Photo` tab; `collection.error` is specified into `StageHead`, which §11 moves into the `Photo` tab on phone; the AI error is inside a dialog that may be closed. So the brief's 'when the photo fails to load' resolves to: nothing visibly happens. Fix inside this design: `app__notice` already exists in §8.1 and is otherwise unused — make it the single home for store-level errors on phone (fixed under the app bar, `--c-danger`, `role="alert"`, with a `Hide` button, the copy for which §9.1 already has), and mark the owning tab. The picture-load failure in particular belongs in the stage, not in the plan.

§8.5, §8.12 and §12 — two first-level features have no phone layout at all, in the round whose stated purpose was the phone. The step walk (§8.5) 'replaces the viewbar inside the stage': head + 56 px Previous/Next + a segmented three-option view + a hint line + the `Mix`/`Paint`/`Then` lines + the warning is roughly 250 px, added to a sticky region that §4.1 already overspends, and §4.1's diagram contains no step row and no reduced canvas height for it (desktop gets `calc(100dvh - 22rem)`; phone gets nothing). This is the layer-mode painting screen — the thing the painter uses with a brush in hand. The close-up strip has the same problem: §4.2 lists it in the iPad stage and §12 puts it 'Stage: close-up tray', but §4.1's phone region ends at the readout, so on a phone the tray has no home. Specify both as phone screens: the step walk as a full-height panel region under a reduced canvas with its own bottom-pinned Previous/Next, and the close-up strip as a row inside the `Photo` tab, with the active detail named in the readout.
shouldFix: §13.4 is false as written, and §9 proves it. 'No `title` attribute carries information that is not also visible as text', but §9 claims to list every string and omits several that today exist only in tooltips: 'An estimate from one swatch: test the wash on a scrap first' (`LayerSteps.vue:31`, `LayerList.vue:36`, a painting-accuracy caveat, not chrome), 'Distance to the photo: 4.2' (`LayerArea.vue:16`, the number behind 'Match: good'), '2 coats on 14% of the image' (`LayerList.vue:52`), 'It brings the picture 1.2 closer to the photo' (`LayerList.vue:122`), the per-wash dilution and share (`PaletteList.vue:65`), and, in `PaintChip.vue`, `nameDe` plus the free-text stock `note` — `nameDe` has no other surface anywhere in the app. Either give each a visible home or add a line in §12 saying it is deliberately dropped. Do not assert the criterion and leave the strings out of the inventory.

§6.1 contrast — the four published ratios are correct (I checked `--c-copy-light` at 6.4:1 and `--c-corporate` at 8.7:1 on white), but they cover only token-on-token pairs. The text that is hardest to read in this app sits on paint colours: `plan__part-text`, the wash letters and the paint chip's number and name, all coloured by `contrastText()` in `src/lib/color.js`, which is a binary black/white switch at OKLab L > 0.68 and guarantees nothing near 4.5:1 for mid-lightness paints. §8.11 then adds a *smaller* second line (`--fs-mini`, 12–13 px) on that same arbitrary background. Specify the rule: minimum text size on a swatch, and either a three-way ink choice or a 1 px `--c-surface` plate behind the text. Deleting the sentence 'Everything clears 4.5:1' would also be honest.

Safe areas contradict themselves. §5 says `env(safe-area-inset-*)` is respected on the app bar, the tab bar and the main padding, but every concrete value in §4.1 omits it: `.app__bar { height: 3.25rem }`, `.app__stage { top: 3.25rem }`, and `.app__main` padding-top `calc(3.25rem + var(--gap-05x))` with no inset term. In the native Tintmap web view (`lib/native.js`, `isNative`) that puts the bar and the sticky stage under the status bar. Write the insets into the values.

§8.8 — the steppers re-run the analysis once per tap, and the spec says so approvingly. `ControlsPanel.vue:118` binds `@change="analysis.analyse()"`, which on a range input fires once per drag; on a stepper it fires per tap, so moving `Colours` from 20 to 32 queues twelve worker runs that the §5 busy rule explicitly refuses to disable. On an iPad with gloves that is twelve flickers and no way to tell which taps landed. Specify: the stepper updates the value and the readout immediately, and calls `analyse()` after about 400 ms of no further taps; the status slot reads `Analysing…` only when the run actually starts.

§5 and §8.3 — the tap-to-place close-up frame does not fit on the device it was designed for. 'A frame of 40 % of the shorter side' on a phone canvas of about 300x200 CSS px is roughly 80 px square, with four `3rem` (48 px) corner handles on it: the handles overlap each other and cover the frame they are meant to adjust. §9.2 has the copy 'That frame is too small.' but no number. State a minimum frame edge of at least 3x the handle size (144 px), place handles outside the frame edge, and if the canvas cannot hold that, specify the phone fallback — e.g. a fixed-proportion frame moved by dragging its middle, with `Use this detail` / `Cancel` in the banner as already specified.

Three contradictions between sections, each one an implementer guess. (a) `Account`: §4.1 puts it in the phone app bar, §2.3, §9.5 and §12 put it 'phone: end of the Settings tab'. (b) The image name: §4.1's diagram shows 'Meadow (sample)' in the phone stage, §11 says `StageHead` renders in the `Photo` tab on phone. (c) The same diagram labels the framing button 'Detail' where §8.2 and §9.2 call it 'Pick a detail', and omits the layer-mode fourth button 'Paint step by step' that §8.2 adds to that row — three text buttons plus a status slot will not fit across 375 px, and no wrap or scroll behaviour is given.

Undefined elements and states that are listed as if specified: `detail__washes` appears in §8.7's element list and is never described anywhere (it is the obvious home for the per-wash dilution lost from `PaletteList.vue:65`); `plan__note`, `plan__empty-actions`, `picture__banner` overflow, and `picture__readout` overflow (the framing banner's 57-character line plus a `Cancel` button in a 3rem bar at 343 px is three lines) all need a stated wrap or truncation rule. On phone, `detail__close` with the copy `Close` sits inside a tab panel — say what it closes, or make it `Clear selection`.

The free-account limit is undesigned, though the brief names it. `pro.js` gates at `FREE_PAINTS = 8`, `FREE_BOXES = 1` and `FREE_IMAGES = 0` in the browser, so a free browser user hits the plan dialog on `Save` and on the ninth paint chip. §8.11 and §8.14 give the paint box no locked chip state, no '8 of 54' counter and no copy; §8.9 defines `:disabled` generically and `PaintChip.vue` already uses its `disabled` prop for an unrelated reason. Specify what a gated chip and a gated `Save` look like before they are tapped.

§10 and §11 — dropping `html { font-size: 10px }` changes the printed sheet even though the legend CSS has no `rem`. Printed A4 at 96 dpi is about 794 px wide, so the `>= 48rem` step in the §6.2 ramp applies and `--fs-copy` becomes 17 px where today's print text is 14 px. Pin it: `@media print` sets an explicit body size and neutralises the ramp. §13.9 asserts print renders as today; make the CSS make that true.

§14.3 is right and should be decided now rather than deferred: `Details` is used for the variety slider, for close-ups ('Detail 2', 'Pick a detail') and for the AI's 'details to keep', all on screen together. Rename the slider `Variety` in this specification. One ambiguous word used three ways in one interface is a defect, not a matter of taste the owner has lived with.
verdict: The strongest of the structural work I have seen in this round, undone by the one thing it was written to fix. §2.2's single plan model genuinely dissolves the mix/layer split rather than repainting it, §9 leaves no string to invent, §5 pairs every removed gesture with a real fallback, and §11 is a buildable migration plan that names actual files. Against that: the phone section rests on an arithmetic error. §4.1 makes four chrome bands sticky above the panel region and §14.2 reports the leftover as "roughly 300 px" when the spec's own numbers give about 95 px on a 390x844 iPhone — so §3.3's "both are on screen at once" is a claim about a screenshot nobody rendered, and §4.2 repeats the failure on the iPad, which the brief calls the primary device. The dark-mode primary button, as §8.9 and §6.1 define it, is white on light blue at about 2:1, in a document whose §6.1 states that everything clears 4.5:1. Accessibility ends at the focus ring: no element semantics for the numbered plan row the brief asked about by name, no live region for the busy state or the readout, state carried in colour alone in the three places that matter, and §13's acceptance criteria contradicted by §5 (40 px wash segments) and by §9 (tooltip copy with no new home). The layer-mode step walk and the close-up tray — both first-level features — have no phone layout at all. This is a document that is precise where precision was easy and confident where it was not measured. The bones are worth keeping; the phone has to be laid out again with the stack added up, and the dark palette has to be checked rather than asserted.
